title: How Aerogel Blankets Are Made: From Sol-Gel Chemistry to Flexible Industrial Insulation
content:
Aerogel blankets are among the most widely recognized commercial aerogel products because they translate a laboratory material into a flexible form that can be installed on pipes, vessels, equipment, and building components. For buyers and engineers, however, the finished blanket often hides the complexity of the manufacturing route behind it. Understanding that route matters: process choices influence mechanical robustness, thermal performance, dusting behavior, hydrophobicity, thickness tolerance, and ultimately project economics.

This article provides a practical overview of how silica aerogel blankets are typically produced. It focuses on the industrial process logic rather than proprietary recipes, using conservative, public-source descriptions. Exact chemistries and line configurations vary by manufacturer, but the main steps are consistent across the sector.

Why aerogel blankets matter in the market

Aerogels are highly porous solids derived from a gel in which the liquid phase is removed while preserving much of the nanostructured network. In commercial insulation markets, the most established format is not a fragile monolith but a fiber-reinforced blanket. This product form combines low thermal conductivity associated with silica aerogel with the handling advantages of a fibrous mat.

That combination is important in industrial insulation, energy infrastructure, process plants, offshore systems, and selected building applications. Compared with rigid specialty forms, blankets are easier to cut, wrap, transport, and install in field conditions. For that reason, the blanket format has become the reference point for many real-world aerogel deployments.

The basic manufacturing concept

At a high level, an aerogel blanket is made by creating a silica gel within or around a reinforcing fiber matrix, then removing the pore liquid in a way that preserves the extremely porous structure. The blanket is subsequently treated, dried if needed, converted, and packaged for sale.

Although public descriptions differ in wording, the process can be simplified into five stages:

  • Preparation of a silica sol or precursor system
  • Impregnation of a fiber batting or nonwoven reinforcement
  • Gelation and aging to build a stable porous network
  • Solvent exchange and drying through supercritical or other controlled routes
  • Surface treatment, finishing, quality control, and converting into rolls or sheets

Step 1: Building the silica precursor system

Most commercial aerogel blankets are based on silica chemistry. Public literature commonly describes silica aerogel formation using alkoxide precursors such as tetraethyl orthosilicate or sodium silicate / waterglass-based routes, depending on cost structure and process design. In both cases, the aim is to form a wet gel containing a connected silica network and a liquid-filled pore system.

The precursor chemistry affects several downstream decisions. Alkoxide systems are well known in aerogel research and can yield high-quality networks, while sodium silicate routes can offer cost advantages and have long been studied for larger-scale manufacturing. Industrial producers may also use catalysts, pH control, additives, and tailored solvent systems to steer gel time and pore development.

Why this stage matters for buyers

Even though customers do not usually purchase chemistry, precursor choice can influence consistency, impurity profile, process cost, and scale-up practicality. When a supplier claims a major cost or sustainability advantage, it is often tied in part to this upstream chemistry and solvent management strategy.

Step 2: Impregnating the fiber reinforcement

A standalone silica aerogel monolith is typically too brittle for demanding field installation. To solve that, manufacturers integrate aerogel with a fibrous reinforcement, often a glass fiber mat or similar nonwoven substrate designed to provide flexibility and dimensional stability.

In a common blanket-making approach, the fiber batting is impregnated with the silica sol so that gel formation occurs throughout the porous reinforcement. The goal is not simply to coat the surface, but to distribute silica throughout the internal volume in a controlled way. Uniform impregnation is important because local variations can affect thermal behavior, thickness, dusting, and bend performance.

Manufacturing challenges at this stage include wetting the reinforcement evenly, avoiding large voids, controlling line speed, and keeping the blanket processable before gelation locks the structure in place.

Step 3: Gelation and aging

Once the precursor is in the reinforcement, the sol transitions into a gel. During gelation, a connected silica network forms and spans the blanket structure. The material is still “wet” at this point because the pores remain filled with liquid.

After gelation, the material is usually aged. Aging is a critical but often overlooked step in aerogel manufacturing. Public technical literature describes aging as a means to strengthen the silica network through continued condensation and structural reorganization. Without adequate aging, the network may shrink excessively or crack during later processing.

For industrial blanket production, aging conditions have to balance throughput with network development. Longer or more controlled aging may improve structural integrity, but it also adds time, solvent handling, and cost.

What engineers should infer from this stage

If two blanket products look similar in datasheets, they may still differ in how robustly the aerogel network was developed before drying. This can show up in practical differences such as resilience during handling, performance retention after installation, or behavior under repeated thermal cycling.

Step 4: Solvent exchange and surface modification

Before drying, manufacturers often perform solvent exchange. This replaces the original pore liquid with a fluid more compatible with the drying process. In aerogel science, solvent exchange is important because capillary forces generated during liquid removal can collapse the pore structure if not properly managed.

Manufacturers may also introduce surface modification at this stage, especially to make silica aerogel hydrophobic. Hydrophobic treatment is commercially important because untreated silica can attract moisture, while insulation buyers often want materials that resist liquid water uptake in service conditions. Public descriptions of commercial aerogel blankets frequently emphasize hydrophobicity as a key feature, especially in industrial and building-envelope use cases.

Step 5: Drying without destroying the nanostructure

Drying is the defining technical challenge in aerogel production. If a wet gel is simply evaporated under ordinary conditions, capillary forces can cause major shrinkage or collapse. Aerogel manufacturing therefore uses specialized drying approaches intended to preserve the porous network.

Supercritical drying

Supercritical drying is the classic aerogel route and remains central to many high-performance silica aerogel processes. In this method, the pore liquid is brought above its critical point so there is no liquid-vapor interface creating capillary stress in the conventional sense. Carbon dioxide is widely discussed in public literature as a practical supercritical drying medium after suitable solvent exchange.

From a manufacturing perspective, supercritical drying can help preserve low density and pore structure, but it requires pressure-rated equipment, solvent handling discipline, cycle-time control, and associated capital investment. This is one reason blanket manufacturing know-how can be difficult to replicate at commercial scale.

Ambient-pressure drying and related routes

Not all silica aerogel products rely on the same drying philosophy. Public research and patent literature describe ambient-pressure drying approaches that use surface modification and process control to reduce collapse during solvent removal. These routes are attractive because they may reduce dependence on high-pressure equipment, although tradeoffs can exist in shrinkage management, process complexity, or final material properties.

For buyers evaluating broad aerogel claims, the main point is simple: “aerogel” does not imply a single manufacturing route. Drying technology is one of the major distinctions behind product cost and scale.

Step 6: Finishing, converting, and quality control

After drying, the blanket may undergo trimming, lamination or facing steps, thermal stabilization, dust reduction measures, cutting to thickness or width, and roll conversion for shipment. Manufacturers also perform quality checks covering dimensions, density, thermal conductivity, hydrophobic behavior, and handling characteristics. Depending on the end market, additional testing may include compression behavior, fire-related performance, or resistance to service temperatures.

This finishing stage is commercially significant. A well-made aerogel blanket is not just an aerogel-filled mat; it is a convertable insulation product that must survive packaging, transport, fabrication, and installation while maintaining enough consistency for project specifications.

How process choices affect real-world product differences

For procurement teams, the process overview becomes useful when comparing vendors. Several visible product differences often trace back to manufacturing decisions:

  • Flexibility: influenced by reinforcement architecture, aerogel loading, and drying outcomes
  • Dusting and cleanliness: influenced by network integrity, surface treatment, and finishing
  • Hydrophobicity: influenced by post-treatment chemistry and process control
  • Thickness consistency: influenced by impregnation uniformity and converting quality
  • Cost structure: influenced by precursor route, solvent recovery, drying method, and production scale

That is why buyers should be cautious about treating all aerogel blankets as interchangeable. Similar branding language can mask meaningful process differences.

Questions buyers and engineers should ask suppliers

Most manufacturers will not disclose proprietary recipes, but they should be able to answer process-oriented questions at a useful level. Examples include:

  • Is the product silica aerogel blanket reinforced with glass fiber or another substrate?
  • Is the blanket designed for industrial hot insulation, cryogenic service, building applications, or multiple use cases?
  • Is the product hydrophobic, and how is that verified in quality control?
  • What is the typical product form: rolls, sheets, composites, or faced systems?
  • What certifications or third-party test methods support the thermal and physical claims?
  • How does the supplier manage lot-to-lot consistency at commercial scale?

Why this topic matters for the aerogel supply chain

Aerogel blankets sit at the intersection of materials science and industrial converting. They are not simply “advanced insulation”; they are engineered composite products whose value depends on repeatable manufacturing. For distributors, OEMs, project engineers, and business development teams, understanding the process helps in three ways: it improves supplier qualification, clarifies application fit, and makes it easier to interpret competing product claims.

It also explains why aerogel blanket production has historically concentrated among a limited number of technically capable manufacturers. Scaling gel chemistry, fiber impregnation, solvent management, drying, and roll goods conversion into a reliable commercial operation is materially harder than making a small aerogel sample in a lab.

Conclusion

The commercial success of aerogel blankets comes from turning a delicate nanoporous material into a flexible insulation product that works in real installations. The path from silica precursor to finished roll involves careful control of gel formation, reinforcement impregnation, aging, solvent exchange, drying, and finishing. Each stage affects product behavior in ways that matter to buyers.

For the aerogel industry, that is the key takeaway: blanket performance is not just about the word “aerogel.” It is about the manufacturing route behind the blanket and the quality discipline used to deliver it at scale.
